title: "Computational model of aesthetics"
description: "Aesthetic preferences as optimizing a behavioral policy to sample the gradient of a perceptual prior."
toc-depth: 3
---

::: {#key-ideas .callout-note title="Key ideas"}
- Aesthetic preferences are modeled as the outcome of optimizing an intrinsic
  (behavioral) policy to sample trajectories for estimating the gradient of a
  perceptual prior, without defining the subjective experience of beauty.
- Building on the [POMDP agent architecture](pomdp-rl.qmd#model-components) and
  the [efficient-encoding motivation for a perceptual
  prior](perceptual-representations.qmd#efficient-encoding-and-the-perceptual-prior),
  the model freezes a useful encoder and separates an extrinsic task policy from
  an intrinsic sampling policy whose trajectories help fit the prior to latents
  encountered under the extrinsic policy.
- The primary candidate model optimizes the intrinsic policy with vanilla
  behavioral policy optimization (BPO) using the gradient of the trajectory-wide
  total negative log-likelihood of the predictive prior; a reverse-KL
  intrinsic-reward alternative is developed on a separate page.
:::

## Overview

Within the [POMDP research project](pomdp-rl.qmd), this model starts from a
fixed, useful perceptual encoder $F$ and asks how an organism efficiently learns
the normalized perceptual prior $R_\theta(z)$ motivated by code-complexity
control in [Perceptual representations and efficient
encoding](perceptual-representations.qmd#efficient-encoding-and-the-perceptual-prior).
Its central thesis is that aesthetic preferences arise from optimizing a
behavioral (intrinsic) policy to sample trajectories that efficiently estimate
the gradient of that perceptual prior. Rather than trying to define the
subjective experience of beauty, the model targets the behavioral preferences
induced by optimizing this sampling policy.

This page builds directly on the shared [POMDP model
components](pomdp-rl.qmd#model-components)---hidden state $s_t$, observation
density $E$, fixed encoder $F$, memory update $U$, and transition model $T$---by
splitting control into two policies acting on $(z_t, h_t)$:

- **Extrinsic policy $\pi_e$:** optimizes ordinary task return and determines
  the distribution of perceptual latents that $R_\theta$ should predict.
- **Intrinsic policy $\pi_i$:** acts as the behavioral sampling policy optimized
  to estimate the gradient of $R_\theta$, hypothesized to produce aesthetic
  preferences.

**First-version scope:** following the POMDP baseline, $F$ and $R_\theta$ have
no explicit temporal-history input, while $\pi_e$ and $\pi_i$ use current
perceptual latents $z_t$ and memory $h_t$. Learning also accumulates past
experience in model parameters. Future models may condition $F$ and $R_\theta$
on memory.

**Model status:** conceptual hypothesis. The mathematical variance-reduction
identities are distinct from the proposed aesthetic mechanism and from the
biological coding-efficiency interpretation discussed in [Perceptual
representations and efficient encoding](perceptual-representations.qmd).

## Primary candidate model: vanilla BPO for the prior gradient

The extrinsically motivated policy $\pi_e$ plays the role of the target policy
in [behavioral policy optimization (BPO)](behavioral-policy-optimization.qmd)
[@papini2024], and the intrinsically motivated policy $\pi_i$ plays the role of
the behavioral policy. What changes from standard BPO is the vector expectation
being estimated: instead of the policy gradient of task return, $\pi_i$ samples
trajectories to estimate the gradient used to fit the predictive perceptual
prior $R_\theta$ to latents encountered under $\pi_e$. Under the page's thesis,
aesthetic preferences reflect the behavioral policy $\pi_i$ obtained from this
optimization.

Consider a trajectory of $N$ decision steps from the [POMDP interaction
loop](pomdp-rl.qmd#stimuli-as-consequences-of-actions),

$$
  \tau = (s_0,x_0,z_0,a_0,\dots,a_{N-1},s_N,x_N,z_N),
$$

generated under either policy $\pi \in \{\pi_e,\pi_i\}$ with the same initial
state distribution $\mu_0$, initial memory $h_0$, observation density $E$, fixed
encoder $F$, memory update $U$, and transition model $T$. Write $p_\pi(\tau)$
for the induced trajectory distribution. Hold $\pi_e$, $F$, and the current
prior parameters $\theta$ fixed when optimizing $\pi_i$.

Using the per-step latent surprise $\ell_\theta(z) = -\log R_\theta(z)$, define
the trajectory-wide total negative log-likelihood of the predictive prior by

$$
  \ell_\theta(\tau) = \sum_{t=0}^{N} \ell_\theta(z_t)
                    = \sum_{t=0}^{N} \bigl[-\log R_\theta(z_t)\bigr].
$$

The target prior loss under the extrinsic policy and the single-trajectory
gradient estimate are

$$
  L(\theta) = \mathbb E_{\tau \sim p_{\pi_e}}\bigl[\ell_\theta(\tau)\bigr],
  \qquad
  g_\theta(\tau) = \nabla_\theta \ell_\theta(\tau)
                 = \sum_{t=0}^{N} \nabla_\theta \bigl[-\log R_\theta(z_t)\bigr].
$$

Assuming differentiation under the expectation is valid,
$\mathbb E_{\tau \sim p_{\pi_e}}[g_\theta(\tau)] = \nabla_\theta L(\theta)$.

For a trajectory sampled from the intrinsic policy $\tau \sim p_{\pi_i}$, the
importance-weighted prior-gradient estimate is

$$
  \widehat g(\tau) = w(\tau)g_\theta(\tau),
  \qquad
  w(\tau) = \frac{p_{\pi_e}(\tau)}{p_{\pi_i}(\tau)}
          = \prod_{t=0}^{N-1} \frac{\pi_e(a_t \mid z_t,h_t)}{\pi_i(a_t \mid z_t,h_t)}.
$$

Because $\mu_0$, $E$, $F$, $U$, and $T$ are shared by both policies, they cancel
from the trajectory density ratio, leaving only the product of known action
probabilities. Whenever $p_{\pi_i}(\tau) > 0$ on every trajectory with
$p_{\pi_e}(\tau)g_\theta(\tau) \ne 0$ (for instance, when
$\pi_e(\cdot \mid z,h) \ll \pi_i(\cdot \mid z,h)$ along reachable $(z,h)$),
the estimator is unbiased:
$\mathbb E_{\tau \sim p_{\pi_i}}[\widehat g(\tau)] = \nabla_\theta L(\theta)$.

Theorem 1 of @papini2024 applies to estimating the expectation of any
vector-valued function [@papini2024, fn. 3; see also @alain2016, Theorem 1].
Among unrestricted trajectory distributions, the one minimizing the trace of the
covariance matrix
$\mathbb E_{\tau \sim q}\bigl[\|\widehat g(\tau) - \nabla_\theta L(\theta)\|_2^2\bigr]$
is

$$
  p_\theta^*(\tau) = \frac{p_{\pi_e}(\tau)\|g_\theta(\tau)\|_2}{C_\theta},
  \qquad
  C_\theta = \mathbb E_{\tau \sim p_{\pi_e}}\bigl[\|g_\theta(\tau)\|_2\bigr],
$$

assuming $0 < C_\theta < \infty$ and finite second moments. Relative to their
probability under $\pi_e$, trajectories whose total prior negative
log-likelihood yields a larger gradient norm are sampled more frequently.

Because the environment dynamics are fixed and $\pi_i$ is restricted to a
parameterized policy class $\Pi$, $p_\theta^*$ is generally not directly
realizable. Vanilla BPO projects $p_\theta^*$ onto the realizable trajectory
distributions by minimizing the forward KL divergence
$D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p_\theta^* \Vert p_{\pi_i})$ [@papini2024, sec. 3.2]. Expanding
$\log p_{\pi_i}(\tau)$ drops every factor independent of $\pi_i$
($\mu_0$, $E$, $F$, $T$), reducing the projection to weighted cross-entropy
minimization [@papini2024, Proposition 3.1]:

$$
  \pi_i^* \in \arg\min_{\pi_i \in \Pi}
  \mathbb E_{\tau \sim p_{\pi_e}}\!\left[
    -\|g_\theta(\tau)\|_2 \sum_{t=0}^{N-1} \log \pi_i(a_t \mid z_t,h_t)
  \right].
$$

Because this expectation is under the extrinsic policy $\pi_e$, it can be
estimated from extrinsic trajectories—or off-policy from previously collected
trajectories using multiple importance sampling [@papini2024, sec. 3.2]—without
estimating unknown latent marginals or constructing a separate step-wise
intrinsic reward for reinforcement learning.

Exact variance reduction relative to on-policy sampling depends on
$\chi^2(p_\theta^* \Vert p_{\pi_i})$ rather than forward KL directly
[@papini2024, Lemma 4.1]. Without defensive sampling, the pure trajectory weight
$w(\tau)$ multiplies across all $N$ steps and can grow large with horizon when
$\pi_i$ diverges from $\pi_e$. Following vanilla BPO [@papini2024, Algorithm 1,
Theorem 2], collecting prior-update trajectories from a defensive mixture
$\Phi = \beta p_{\pi_e} + (1 - \beta)p_{\pi_i}$ with $\beta \in (0,1]$
guarantees support coverage and relates excess gradient variance to
$D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p_\theta^* \Vert p_{\pi_i})$. For $\tau \sim \Phi$, the
applied importance weight is

$$
  w_\Phi(\tau) = \frac{p_{\pi_e}(\tau)}{\Phi(\tau)}
               = \left[\beta + (1 - \beta)
                 \prod_{t=0}^{N-1} \frac{\pi_i(a_t \mid z_t,h_t)}{\pi_e(a_t \mid z_t,h_t)}
                 \right]^{-1}
               \le \frac{1}{\beta}
$$

whenever $p_{\pi_e}(\tau) > 0$ (and $w_\Phi(\tau) = 0$ when $p_{\pi_e}(\tau) = 0$).
Although $w_\Phi(\tau)$ stays bounded by $1/\beta$ at every horizon, the
$N$-step action-probability product inside it can still concentrate weights near
$0$ or $1/\beta$ over long horizons if $\pi_i$ departs sharply from $\pi_e$,
reducing effective sample size and the variance reduction available from the
intrinsic component. Furthermore, minimizing single-update gradient variance
does not account for correlations across successive prior updates.

## Alternative candidate: reverse-KL intrinsic reward

An alternative formulation replaces trajectory-level forward KL with an RL
intrinsic reward defined over single-step latent marginals $p_\pi(z)$, whose
expected value under $\pi_i$ minimizes reverse KL divergence
$D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p_{\pi_i} \Vert q_\theta^*)$ to the single-sample optimal
latent proposal. Because the ratio of extrinsic to intrinsic latent marginals is
unknown, that approach requires a separate density-ratio estimator and inherits
the support-coverage caveats of reverse KL. See [Reverse-KL intrinsic reward for
prior sampling](reverse-kl-prior-sampling.qmd) for the full derivation and
feature-based ratio estimator.

## Future extension: temporal conditioning

If a future version conditions the encoder and perceptual prior on memory as
$F(z_t \mid x_t,h_t)$ and $R_\theta(z_t \mid h_t)$ (see [Perceptual
representations and efficient
encoding](perceptual-representations.qmd#future-extension-temporal-conditioning)),
replacing $R_\theta(z_t)$ with $R_\theta(z_t \mid h_t)$ inside
$\ell_\theta(\tau)$ leaves the trajectory importance weights $w(\tau)$ and
$w_\Phi(\tau)$ unchanged because $h_t$ is already determined along the
trajectory. Conditioning the prior on memory could capture sequence expectations
and order effects, including those important in music.

## Open questions

- **BPO and horizon scaling:** how do horizon $N$, policy-class expressiveness
  $\Pi$, defensive weight $\beta$, and sample allocation between $\pi_e$ and
  $\pi_i$ affect prior-gradient variance and learning speed? When does
  trajectory-level importance weighting outperform unweighted or on-policy prior
  learning?
- **Policy scheduling:** when should the agent act under $\pi_e$ versus $\pi_i$,
  and how should $\pi_i$ track simultaneous updates to both $\pi_e$ and
  $\theta$?
- **Behavioral link to aesthetics:** which empirical signatures of aesthetic
  preference emerge from optimizing $\pi_i$ for prior-gradient sampling, and how
  does this account compare with compression-progress and predictive-processing
  theories [@schmidhuber2009; @brielmann2022]?
- **Temporal extension:** how does conditioning $R_\theta$ on memory $h_t$ alter
  the trajectories favored by $\pi_i$ in sequential domains?

## Evidence and source coverage

The hypothesis that aesthetic preferences arise from behavioral policy
optimization for a perceptual prior is a conceptual hypothesis. Mathematical
variance-reduction identities from BPO support the trajectory-sampling mechanism
without establishing that it accounts for human or biological aesthetics, and
the coding-cost motivation for learning $R_\theta$ is evaluated separately in
[Perceptual representations and efficient
encoding](perceptual-representations.qmd).

This behavioral-sampling account sits alongside compression-progress and
predictive-processing theories of aesthetics [@schmidhuber2009; @brielmann2022],
while avoiding a definition of subjective beauty. Further literature analysis
and empirical testing are needed to establish its precise relationship to those
theories.

**Topics:** computational aesthetics; behavioral policy optimization; importance
sampling; attention; reinforcement learning; perceptual prior.
